Female Moustached flowerpiercers ultimately attain an adult body mass of 16.2 grams [Wwi = 16.2 grams], a figure consistent with the relatively small size characteristic of thraupid flowerpiercers inhabiting high-elevation cloud forests. In contrast, the mass at hatching is considerably lower; field measurements indicate that newly emerged chicks weigh approximately 2.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.3 grams], representing roughly fourteen percent of the maternal body mass, a ratio that aligns with the altricial development strategy typical of most passerine birds. The incubation period required for embryonic development under controlled thermal conditions at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] was recorded as 12 days [ab = 12 days], a value that was estimated based on comparative data from the congeneric species Diglossa cyanea. This relatively brief incubation interval reflects the rapid organogenesis and yolk-dependent growth characteristic of small-bodied tropical songbirds, which face strong selective pressure to minimize nest predation risk during the egg stage.

First feeding of the altricial nestling is followed by a period of rapid mass gain and feather development within the nest. The time since birth at fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest cavity, was determined to be 13 days [tx = 13 days] in individuals maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value again derived from observations of Diglossa cyanea. This short nestling phase, lasting less than two weeks, is notable among high-altitude passerines and suggests a strategy of accelerated development to escape the dangers of a thermally demanding and predator-rich microhabitat. The downy chick progresses through the pin-feathered and nestling bird stages with remarkable speed, likely supported by intensive biparental provisioning of insects and nectar.

Gonadal maturation, or the onset of puberty, occurs relatively late in the development of this species. The time since birth at puberty was documented as 45 days [tp = 45 days] when measured under the same thermoneutral conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This interval of approximately six weeks after hatching represents the period required for the reproductive system to become functionally active, enabling the individual to progress from an immature bird to a sexually mature adult capable of gametogenesis. The 45-day pubertal delay is intermediate among its congeners and likely reflects the energetic demands associated with reaching the asymptotic body mass of 16.2 grams [Wwi = 16.2 grams] for females, a prerequisite for the substantial investment in egg production. The growing juvenile thus undergoes a sustained phase of pre-reproductive development before initiating reproductive activity.

First reproduction among Moustached flowerpiercers is deferred considerably beyond the attainment of sexual maturity. The time since birth at first brood was estimated at 401.5 days [tR = 401.5 days] under a sustained thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This first successful breeding event, occurring roughly 13 months after hatching, represents the initiation of the bird's reproductive career and is characterized by the laying of the inaugural clutch. The long delay between puberty and first reproduction suggests that habitat quality, territory acquisition, and the establishment of a stable pair bond are critical factors shaping the onset of nesting activity in this species. Females lay a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt], with the capacity to produce up to 2.5 successful clutches each year [F_R_i = up to 2.5 successful clutches each year], a maximum reproductive rate that reflects the trade-off between fecundity and the intense parental care demands of provisioning nestlings at high altitudes.

The maximum lifespan recorded in the wild for Diglossa mystacalis was estimated at 3,942 days [am = 3,942 days] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value again based on extrapolations from the closely related Diglossa cyanea. This longevity, equivalent to nearly 10.8 years, is remarkably high for a passerine of such modest body mass and suggests a slow life-history pace typical of tropical montane birds, which often exhibit reduced extrinsic mortality rates. Correspondingly, the resting metabolic rate of the species was measured as a maximum oxygen consumption of 34.55 milliliters per hour [JOi = 34.55 milliliters per hour] under the same thermoneutral temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption, representing the energetic cost of sustaining vital physiological functions in a post-absorptive, resting state, is consistent with the relatively low mass-specific metabolic rates observed among thraupid finches inhabiting cool, high-elevation environments with predictable resource availability. Expressed on a daily basis, this translates to a maximum daily reproduction rate of about 2.5 offspring per year [Ri = about 2.5 offspring per year], a rate that aligns with the constraint of single-egg clutches in a seasonally brief breeding window typical of high-altitude neotropical songbirds.
